cls: Oral iron supplement (chelated ferrous iron, amino-acid chelate)
pharm: Iron replacement for treatment and prevention of iron deficiency and iron-deficiency anaemia; provides elemental iron in a glycine-chelated form with high bioavailability and reduced GI irritation.
quick: Typically 14-28 mg elemental iron once daily for prophylaxis; up to 50-100 mg elemental iron/day for treatment of deficiency
Best absorbed on an empty stomach; may take with food if GI upset; avoid tea/coffee/dairy/antacids around dosing
Iron supplementation commonly used in pregnancy to treat/prevent deficiency; compatible at recommended doses
Compatible; iron is a normal milk constituent and supplementation is acceptable
Use with caution in CKD; iron status (ferritin, TSAT) should guide therapy
Avoid iron overload in hepatic disease; monitor in conditions with iron loading
Chronic alcohol use can increase iron absorption/storage; avoid excess
Haemoglobin, serum ferritin, transferrin saturation; reticulocyte response
summary: Ferrous bisglycinate is an amino-acid (glycine) chelate of ferrous iron used to treat and prevent iron deficiency and iron-deficiency anaemia. Each iron atom is bound to two glycine molecules, which is reported to improve absorption and reduce the gastrointestinal irritation typical of conventional ferrous salts. Doses are expressed in terms of elemental iron and depend on whether the goal is prophylaxis or correction of established deficiency. Absorption is best on an empty stomach and is enhanced by vitamin C; tea, coffee, dairy, antacids and certain medicines reduce uptake. The main risks are gastrointestinal intolerance, constipation, dark stools, and accidental overdose in children, which can be life-threatening.
indications: Prevention of iron deficiency in at-risk groups (pregnancy, menstruating women, infants/children, vegetarians, blood donors, malabsorption)
Iron supplementation when dietary intake is inadequate

dosage.d: Approximately 50-100 mg elemental iron daily, in single or divided doses, until haemoglobin normalises
dosage.n: Continue 3 months after Hb normalises to replenish stores; dose expressed as elemental iron

dosage.d: Approximately 14-28 mg elemental iron once daily
dosage.n: Adjust to local guidelines and iron status

dosage.d: Per paediatric guidance; typically expressed as mg elemental iron/kg/day
dosage.n: Keep out of reach of children; overdose can be fatal

admin: Take orally, preferably on an empty stomach (1 hour before or 2 hours after meals) for best absorption
Take with food if gastrointestinal upset occurs, accepting reduced absorption
Separate from tea, coffee, milk/dairy, calcium and antacids by at least 2 hours
Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) or orange juice can enhance iron absorption
Swallow tablets/capsules whole with water; do not exceed the recommended dose
moa: Iron is an essential element required for haemoglobin synthesis and oxygen transport, as well as for myoglobin and various iron-dependent enzymes. Supplemental ferrous (Fe2+) iron is absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, transported into enterocytes, and either stored as ferritin or released to plasma transferrin for delivery to the bone marrow and other tissues. In ferrous bisglycinate, iron is chelated by two glycine molecules, which is reported to protect the iron during transit and present it for absorption via amino-acid and divalent-metal pathways, improving uptake and tolerability compared with simple ferrous salts.

absolute: Anaemias not caused by iron deficiency (e.g., haemolytic, sideroblastic, thalassaemia without deficiency) unless iron deficiency is also present
Known hypersensitivity to iron salts or excipients
relative: Active peptic ulcer disease, regional enteritis, ulcerative colitis (may aggravate)
monitor: Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation to avoid overload

preg: Iron requirements increase in pregnancy and supplementation is widely used to treat and prevent iron deficiency and iron-deficiency anaemia. Ferrous bisglycinate at recommended doses is considered compatible; tailor dose to iron status and local antenatal guidance.
lact: Iron is a normal constituent of breast milk and oral iron supplementation during lactation is acceptable. Maternal supplementation is used to correct maternal deficiency; weigh need against avoidance of overload.
renal: Use with caution in chronic kidney disease, where anaemia is multifactorial and iron status must be assessed (ferritin, transferrin saturation). Oral iron absorption may be reduced; intravenous iron is often preferred in advanced CKD. Avoid iron overload.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is established, but iron can accumulate in hepatic disease and in conditions with iron loading. Avoid in haemochromatosis and monitor iron indices in chronic liver disease.

major: Iron overload risk if combined with parenteral iron or multiple iron products
Reduced absorption of levothyroxine, levodopa, methyldopa, penicillamine and bisphosphonates - separate dosing
moderate: Tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones - iron chelates and reduces antibiotic absorption; separate by at least 2-3 hours
Antacids, proton-pump inhibitors and H2 blockers - reduce iron absorption
Calcium and magnesium salts - reduce iron absorption
minor: Mycophenolate and some antiretrovirals - reduced absorption; separate dosing
interactions.food: Tea, coffee, eggs, milk/dairy, whole-grain cereals and foods rich in phytates or polyphenols reduce iron absorption; vitamin C-containing foods enhance it.
interactions.alcohol: Chronic excessive alcohol increases iron absorption and storage and may promote iron overload; avoid excess.
interactions.diagnostics: Can darken stools and may cause false-positive results on tests for occult blood (guaiac); raises serum iron and ferritin.

serious: Acute iron overdose (especially in children) with corrosive GI injury, metabolic acidosis, shock and hepatic injury
Iron overload with chronic excessive use
emergency: Accidental iron overdose in a child (medical emergency - seek immediate care)
Severe GI bleeding or signs of bowel injury

monitoring: Haemoglobin and reticulocyte count to confirm response (expect reticulocytosis within 1-2 weeks)
Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation to gauge stores and avoid overload
Periodic full blood count during prolonged therapy
counsel: Take preferably on an empty stomach with water; if it upsets your stomach, take with a little food
Avoid taking with tea, coffee, milk, calcium or antacids - leave at least 2 hours between them
Your stools may turn black - this is harmless; report black tarry stools with stomach pain or unwellness
Keep iron tablets out of sight and reach of children - even a small overdose can be very dangerous to a child
Constipation is common; increase fluids and fibre, and tell your doctor if troublesome
Continue for as long as advised, often a few months after blood counts normalise, to refill iron stores
pk: Reticulocyte response in 3-10 days; symptomatic improvement over 1-2 weeks
Haemoglobin rise typically evident within 2-4 weeks; stores replenish over weeks to months
No fixed plasma half-life; iron is recycled and stored, with very limited physiological excretion
Continue 1-3 months after Hb normalises to restore iron stores
Store in original container at room temperature, protected from moisture; keep away from children
pearls: Faithful supplement entry - doses are always expressed as ELEMENTAL iron; check the elemental content of the product, not the salt weight
Ferrous bisglycinate is a glycine-chelated iron reported to have good bioavailability and better GI tolerability than conventional ferrous sulfate/fumarate
Absorption is best on an empty stomach and with vitamin C; reduced by tea, coffee, dairy, calcium, antacids and PPIs
Continue therapy 1-3 months after haemoglobin normalises to replenish stores
Iron is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in young children - emphasise safe storage
missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember on the same day. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Iron overdose is a medical emergency, particularly in children. Features evolve over hours: vomiting, abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea, then metabolic acidosis, shock, coma, and later hepatic necrosis and GI strictures. Management includes early supportive care, assessment of serum iron, and chelation with deferoxamine for significant ingestions. Seek emergency medical attention immediately for any suspected overdose.
